title: 2020 HMMT Invitational Problem 4
statement:
Let \(C_{k}=\frac{1}{k+1}\binom{2 k}{k}\) denote the \(k^{\text {th }}\) Catalan number and \(p\) be an odd prime. Prove that exactly half of the numbers in the set

\[\left\{\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} C_{k} n^{k} \mid n \in\{1,2, \ldots, p-1\}\right\}\]

are divisible by \(p\).

solutions.text: Solution 1: We work in \(\mathbb{F}_{p}[X]\). We claim that \[(1-4 X)^{\frac{p+1}{2}}-1+2 X^{p}+2 X \sum_{k=0}^{p-1} C_{k} X^{k}=0\] The solution follows from this claim, as \[\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} C_{k} n^{k} \equiv 0 \quad(\bmod p) \Longleftrightarrow(1-4 n)^{\frac{p+1}{2}}-1+2 n^{p}+2 n \equiv 0 \quad(\bmod p)\] Since \(n^{p} \equiv n(\bmod p)\), this is equivalent to \(n \equiv \frac{1}{4}(\bmod p)\) or \(1-4 n\) being a non-zero quadratic residue in \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\). But we must omit the solution of \(n=0\), so we get \(1+\left(\frac{p-1}{2}-1\right)=\frac{p-1}{2}\) values of \(n\) that work. Now we prove the claim. Observe the following facts: - \(C_{p-1}=\frac{1}{2 p-1}\binom{2 p-1}{p}=-1\) by Lucas' theorem. - For \(\frac{p-1}{2}\frac{p+1}{2}\) and \(k=0\) by the above facts, as the coefficient is \(2+2 C_{p-1}\) for \(k=p, 2 C_{k}\) for \(\frac{p+1}{2}
